blocks.content: 1. What is an API?
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274925461-208053268.png
blocks.alt: Every API follows the same pattern, defined input in, predictable output back

blocks.content: API stands for Application Programming Interface. The simplest way to think about it: an API is a defined way for two pieces of software to talk to each other.
One side says "here's what you can send me" the other side sends it and gets a predictable result back.
Think of it like a power socket. You don’t need to know how electricity is made you just plug in and use it. The socket is like an API: a simple interface that hides all the complexity behind it.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: The pattern is always the same:
defined input → predictable output. Whether it's a network request or a function call, the concept is identical.

blocks.content: 2. The request-response model
Every API call follows this loop. Your app sends a request. The server processes it and sends back a response usually JSON.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274931783-773569472.png
blocks.alt: Every API call is the same loop, send a request, the server processes it, a response comes back

blocks.content: 3. HTTP Methods: What Action Are You Taking?

blocks.alt: The four core HTTP methods each represent a different action on a resource

blocks.content: These methods define what kind of operation you want to perform on a server resource.
1. GET

Used to fetch data from the server.
It does not change anything on the server.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274934916-381445361.png
blocks.alt: GET fetches data without changing anything on the server

blocks.content: Example:
You open a website or request user data → you are using GET.
Key points:

["Read-only operation
","Safe (no side effects)
","Can be cached
"]
items: Read-only operation
Safe (no side effects)
Can be cached

blocks.content: 2. POST
Used to create a new resource on the server.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274936444-654523013.png
blocks.alt: POST creates a new resource on the server

blocks.content: Example:
Submitting a form, creating a new user, adding a post.
Key points:

["Creates new data
","Data is sent in the request body
","Not idempotent (calling it multiple times creates multiple resources)
"]

Data is sent in the request body

blocks.content: 3. PUT
Used to update an existing resource completely.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274938149-889069813.png
blocks.alt: PUT replaces an existing resource in full

blocks.content: Example:
Updating a user profile by replacing all fields.
Key points:

["Replaces the entire resource
","Idempotent (same request multiple times → same result)
"]
items: Replaces the entire resource
Idempotent (same request multiple times → same result)

blocks.content: 4. DELETE
Used to remove a resource from the server.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274939724-608772501.png
blocks.alt: DELETE removes a resource from the server

blocks.content: Example:
Deleting a user or removing a post.
Key points:

["Deletes data permanently
","Idempotent (deleting again has no further effect)
"]
items: Deletes data permanently
Idempotent (deleting again has no further effect)

Simple Way to Remember

GET → Read
POST → Create
PUT → Update (full replace)

blocks.content: 5. Types of APIs
APIs can be categorized based on who can access them and how they are used.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274942929-917545723.png
blocks.alt: APIs are categorized as public, private, or library depending on who can access them

blocks.content: APIs can be categorized based on who can access them and how they are used.
1. Public (Open APIs)
Anyone can use them. Companies expose these so developers can build applications on top of their services
examples include Twitter API, OpenWeather, Stripe.
2. Private (Internal APIs)
Used only within a company. Different internal services communicate with each other using these APIs.
example, Amazon’s order, payment, and logistics systems.
3. Library (Code APIs)
These are functions provided by programming languages or frameworks. There is no network call you directly use code like numpy.mean() or str.split().
6. How APIs Communicate
APIs don't all speak the same language. The protocol defines the rules: what format the data is in, how requests are structured, and what the server expects back.

{"headers":["PROTOCOL","FORMAT","BEST FOR","EXAMPLE USE"],"rows":[["REST","JSON","Most web & mobile apps","Instagram, Twitter, Spotify"],["GraphQL","JSON (query)","When client controls shape of data","GitHub, Shopify, Meta"],["gRPC","Protobuf (binary)","Microservice-to-microservice","Google internal systems"],["SOAP","XML","Enterprise / banking / legacy","Bank of America, SAP"]]}
REST is the default choice for most systems you'll design. Simple, stateless, and universally understood.
Only reach for GraphQL, gRPC, or SOAP when REST's limitations are a real problem.

8. APIs in High-Level Design
In system design, APIs are the contracts between services. Before you design the database or pick the infrastructure, you define:

["What APIs does each service expose? 
","What does each service need from others?
"]
items: What APIs does each service expose?
What does each service need from others?

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019237-953376623.png
blocks.alt: In HLD, a client talks to an API gateway, which routes to the right service, which talks to the database

blocks.content: APIs in High-Level Design define how different parts of a system communicate with each other. Instead of thinking about internal code, HLD focuses on the external contract: what requests a component accepts, what responses it returns, and how components are connected.

In the diagram, the flow starts from the client, which could be a mobile app. The client does not directly talk to individual services. It sends an HTTP request to a single entry point called the API Gateway. This gateway acts as the front door of the system.

The API Gateway is responsible for receiving requests, identifying where they should go, and forwarding them to the correct service. For example, a request related to users is routed to the User Service, a request related to orders goes to the Order Service, and a payment request goes to the Payment Service. This routing is based on API paths such as /users, /orders, or /payments.

Each service exposes its own APIs. These are internal or public endpoints that define what operations are allowed. The User Service might expose APIs to create or fetch users, the Order Service handles order creation and retrieval, and the Payment Service processes transactions. These services are usually independent and follow the microservices architecture style.

Once a service processes a request, it interacts with the database if needed. For example, the Order Service might write a new order or read existing order data. After processing, the response flows back through the API Gateway to the client.

From an HLD perspective, APIs are important because they define system boundaries. They allow teams to work independently on different services as long as the API contracts are respected. They also make the system scalable and maintainable because services can evolve without tightly coupling to each other.

In summary, APIs in HLD are not just endpoints. They are the backbone of communication, defining how requests flow from the client through the gateway to services and back, ensuring modularity, scalability, and clear separation of concerns.
9. API Familiarization Only
Got it. This is just a basic exposure to how an API looks, nothing to overthink right now.

At this stage, the only thing to be comfortable with is the idea that a method like this represents an endpoint where a client sends some data and gets something back. The annotations define how the outside world interacts with it, and the method body defines what happens.
We can revisit this later in a much deeper way, including request flow, validation, serialization, gateway routing, and real system design usage.
Request and response are already visible inside this method.
Request is this part:

@PostMapping("/users")
@RequestBody User user
The client sends an HTTP POST request to /users with a JSON body. That JSON body is converted into the User user object. So:
["URL /users → tells where request is going","@PostMapping → tells it is a POST request","@RequestBody User user → this is the incoming request data"]
items: URL /users → tells where request is going
@PostMapping → tells it is a POST request
@RequestBody User user → this is the incoming request data

blocks.content: Response is this part:
return user;
Whatever you return from the method becomes the HTTP response. Here, the same user object is sent back to the client as JSON.
Now what each thing is used for:
@PostMapping("/users")
Defines the API endpoint. It means “this method handles POST requests on /users”.
@RequestBody
Used to take incoming JSON from the client and convert it into a Java object.
User user
This is the request payload object. It holds data sent by the client (like name, email, etc.).
return user
This is the response. Spring automatically converts it back to JSON and sends it to the client.
So in simple terms:

Client sends JSON → goes into @RequestBody User user (request)
Method processes → returns user (response)
